title: Reproductive Hormones and the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, and gonads regulate one another through gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), the sex steroids, inhibin, and prolactin. It covers why GnRH must pulse, how each gonadotropin acts on a different gonadal cell, how estradiol switches from negative to positive feedback, how binding proteins decide free hormone levels, what each steroid does in its target tissues, how puberty starts, and how prolactin shuts the axis down. Board questions usually change one link in the axis and ask you to predict every downstream hormone level, so the goal is to reason through feedback rather than memorize patterns.

connections.how: The enzymes split between theca and granulosa cells, and 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues, are the steroid pathway applied to specific cells.

sections.title: Pulsatile GnRH and why continuous GnRH suppresses the axis

blocks.text: GnRH is a 10 amino acid peptide made by a small population of neurons scattered mainly in the arcuate nucleus and preoptic area of the hypothalamus. Their axons end at the median eminence, where GnRH enters the hypophyseal portal capillaries and reaches the gonadotrophs at high concentration. Because GnRH has a half-life of only a few minutes, each burst produces a sharp rise and fall at the pituitary. In adults the bursts recur about every 1 to 2 hours, more often in the follicular phase and less often in the luteal phase, when progesterone slows the pulse generator.

The GnRH receptor on gonadotrophs is coupled to Gq. Binding activates phospholipase C, which produces inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol; IP3 releases intracellular Ca2+, triggering exocytosis of stored LH and FSH, and protein kinase C drives transcription of the gonadotropin subunit genes. The gap between pulses lets the receptor and its signaling pathway recover. Pulse frequency also steers synthesis: faster pulses favor transcription of the LH beta subunit, and slower pulses favor FSH beta. Slow luteal pulses, together with the fall in inhibin A and estradiol as the corpus luteum regresses, help FSH rise first at the start of a new cycle, while faster pulses before ovulation favor LH.

When GnRH or a long-acting GnRH agonist is present continuously, gonadotrophs first release their stored LH and FSH, causing a flare of gonadotropins and sex steroids over the first one to two weeks. Constant occupancy then uncouples the receptor from Gq signaling and reduces receptor number, so the cells stop responding. LH and FSH fall, and testosterone or estradiol falls to castrate levels, a reversible state often called medical castration. A pump that delivers GnRH in physiologic pulses does the opposite and can restore a dormant axis.

blocks.title: Continuous GnRH exposure to hypogonadism
steps: Continuous GnRH agonist occupies gonadotroph receptors
Stored LH and FSH released: transient flare
Receptors uncouple from Gq and are downregulated
LH and FSH secretion falls
Leydig, theca, and granulosa stimulation is lost
Testosterone or estradiol falls to castrate levels
blocks.caption: The same agonist that stimulates when pulsed suppresses when constant; the flare comes first, suppression follows.

blocks.text: The pattern of GnRH delivery explains several disorders. In Kallmann syndrome, GnRH neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode into the hypothalamus during development, so patients have low LH, FSH, and sex steroids together with anosmia. In functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from energy deficit or stress, the pulse generator slows, giving low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins and low estradiol.

blocks.predict: A man receives a depot GnRH agonist. What happens to his serum testosterone in the first week and after one month?
blocks.explain: Testosterone rises in the first week because stored LH is released (the flare). After about a month, desensitized gonadotrophs secrete little LH, so testosterone falls to castrate levels.

sections.title: The male axis: Leydig and Sertoli cells and their separate feedback loops

blocks.text: LH and FSH act on different cells of the testis. LH binds a Gs-coupled receptor on Leydig cells in the interstitium; cAMP and protein kinase A increase the steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein, which moves cholesterol into mitochondria for the rate-limiting side-chain cleavage step, so testosterone synthesis rises. FSH binds a Gs-coupled receptor on Sertoli cells inside the seminiferous tubules, where it stimulates androgen-binding protein (ABP), inhibin B, and aromatase, and supports the germ cells that Sertoli cells nurse.

Spermatogenesis needs both hormones. Testosterone diffuses from Leydig cells into the tubules, where ABP holds it at a concentration many times higher than in serum (often quoted as about 50 to 100 fold). Sertoli cells, not germ cells, carry the androgen receptor, so testosterone supports spermatogenesis by acting on Sertoli cells.

blocks.title: Two feedback loops of the male axis
steps: Hypothalamus releases GnRH pulses
Pituitary secretes LH and FSH
LH drives Leydig cell testosterone
FSH drives Sertoli cell ABP and inhibin B
Testosterone and estradiol slow GnRH pulses and lower LH
Inhibin B lowers pituitary FSH selectively
blocks.caption: Each gonadotropin is regulated mainly by the product of its own target cell.

blocks.text: Testosterone feeds back at both the hypothalamus, where it slows GnRH pulse frequency, and the pituitary, where it reduces the LH response. Part of this feedback in men is carried by estradiol formed by aromatization of testosterone. Because GnRH stimulates both gonadotropins, testosterone lowers FSH somewhat as well, but the selective brake on FSH is inhibin B, which acts directly on gonadotrophs. These separate loops let a lab panel localize damage, as the table shows.

blocks.title: Predicting male axis labs
rows: Primary testicular failure (for example Klinefelter syndrome)
Selective Sertoli cell or germ cell damage
blocks.caption: Gonadotropins are high when the testis fails and low when the hypothalamus or pituitary fails or is suppressed.

blocks.title: Worked example: exogenous testosterone and infertility
blocks.text: A 28-year-old man using injected testosterone for muscle gain has small, soft testes and azoospermia. Serum testosterone is high, so negative feedback slows GnRH pulses and suppresses LH. Without LH, Leydig cells stop producing testosterone inside the testis, and intratesticular testosterone falls far below the level spermatogenesis requires even though serum testosterone is above normal. FSH and inhibin B are also suppressed, so Sertoli cell support fails. Testicular volume falls because the seminiferous tubules, which form most of the testis, lose their germ cells. The expected labs are high serum testosterone, low LH, low FSH, and low inhibin B.

sections.title: Two-cell ovarian steroidogenesis and the switch to positive feedback

blocks.text: Neither cell type in a follicle can make estradiol alone. Theca interna cells, outside the basement membrane, have LH receptors, access to LDL cholesterol from nearby capillaries, and the enzymes cholesterol side-chain cleavage, 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, and 17-alpha-hydroxylase with 17,20-lyase activity (CYP17). LH stimulation therefore produces androstenedione. Granulosa cells, inside the avascular basement membrane, lack CYP17 but express aromatase when FSH stimulates them. Androstenedione diffuses inward, aromatase converts it to estrone, and 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts estrone to estradiol.

blocks.title: The two-cell model
rows: FSH; LH receptors added late in the dominant follicle
blocks.caption: LH provides androgen substrate in theca cells; FSH provides the aromatase that converts it in granulosa cells.

blocks.text: As the dominant follicle grows, FSH induces LH receptors on its granulosa cells, so the follicle can keep growing while rising estradiol and inhibin B lower FSH and starve the smaller follicles. At low to moderate concentrations, estradiol exerts negative feedback, mainly lowering FSH. When estradiol stays above about 200 pg/mL for about 36 to 48 hours, the hypothalamic and pituitary response reverses. Estradiol now acts through kisspeptin neurons to increase GnRH release and raises gonadotroph GnRH receptor number and sensitivity, so a large LH surge results, with a smaller FSH rise. A small rise in progesterone from luteinizing granulosa cells around the onset of the surge amplifies it.

blocks.title: Follicular phase to ovulation
steps: FSH induces aromatase and growth in the dominant follicle
Estradiol rises; negative feedback lowers FSH
Estradiol above about 200 pg/mL for about 2 days
Feedback switches to positive; GnRH and gonadotroph sensitivity rise
Midcycle LH surge
Oocyte completes meiosis I, arrests at metaphase II
Follicle ruptures about 34 to 36 hours after surge onset
Corpus luteum secretes progesterone, estradiol, and inhibin A
blocks.caption: The follicle times its own ovulation: only a mature follicle makes enough estradiol for long enough to trigger the surge.

blocks.text: The LH surge also induces proteolytic enzymes and prostaglandins that weaken the follicle wall, and it converts granulosa and theca cells into luteal cells. Progesterone from the corpus luteum, together with estradiol and inhibin A, then slows GnRH pulses and suppresses LH and FSH, so the positive feedback state cannot recur in the luteal phase.

blocks.predict: If FSH were absent but LH normal, what would happen to ovarian androgen and estradiol output?
blocks.explain: Theca cells would still make androstenedione under LH, but granulosa cells would lack aromatase and follicles would not mature. Estradiol would be low and no LH surge would occur, while androgen output would be preserved or relatively high.

sections.title: Sex steroid transport, SHBG, and free testosterone

blocks.text: Sex steroids are lipophilic and travel in plasma mostly bound to proteins. In men, about 1 to 3% of testosterone is free, roughly a third to a half is loosely bound to albumin, and the remainder is tightly bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). Women have higher SHBG, so a larger share of their testosterone is SHBG-bound. SHBG binds DHT and testosterone with higher affinity than estradiol. Albumin binds with low affinity and releases hormone readily as blood passes through capillaries, so the free plus albumin-bound fraction, called bioavailable testosterone, determines tissue effect. SHBG-bound hormone is largely unavailable. Progesterone and cortisol are carried mainly by corticosteroid-binding globulin and albumin rather than SHBG.

SHBG is made in the liver, and its synthesis responds to hormones and metabolic state. Estrogen and thyroid hormone increase it; insulin and androgens suppress it. Hyperinsulinemia lowers SHBG directly, which is why obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) are associated with low SHBG.

blocks.title: Factors that change SHBG
blocks.caption: Changes in SHBG alter free hormone fractions before the axis has time to compensate.

blocks.text: The consequence of an SHBG change depends on whether feedback can compensate. In a woman, ovarian and adrenal androgen output is not tightly regulated by serum testosterone, so a fall in SHBG raises free testosterone and can cause hirsutism and acne with a normal total testosterone. In a man with an intact axis, a rise in SHBG first lowers free testosterone; the hypothalamus senses this, LH rises, and total testosterone climbs until free testosterone returns toward normal. Because SHBG binds testosterone more tightly than estradiol, a rise in SHBG also increases the free estradiol to free testosterone ratio, which helps explain gynecomastia in cirrhosis and hyperthyroidism.

blocks.title: Worked example: normal total, high free testosterone
blocks.text: A 24-year-old woman with obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and hirsutism has total testosterone in the upper normal range. Her fasting insulin is high. Insulin suppresses hepatic SHBG synthesis, so SHBG is low and a larger fraction of her testosterone is free. Free testosterone is therefore raised even though the total is normal, and hair follicles and sebaceous glands respond to the free hormone. Insulin also acts with LH on theca cells to increase androgen production. A total testosterone alone would underestimate her androgen exposure; free or bioavailable testosterone, or total testosterone with SHBG, reflects it.

sections.title: Actions of testosterone, DHT, estrogen, and progesterone

blocks.text: Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) act on the same intracellular androgen receptor, a ligand-activated transcription factor. DHT binds it with higher affinity and dissociates more slowly, so it is the more potent androgen. Which hormone acts in a tissue depends on whether that tissue expresses 5-alpha-reductase. The type 2 isoenzyme is concentrated in genital skin, the urogenital sinus and prostate, and scalp and beard hair follicles; the type 1 isoenzyme is found in sebaceous glands and the liver. Testosterone acts directly where 5-alpha-reductase is scarce, and some tissues respond to testosterone after aromatase converts it to estradiol.

blocks.title: Target tissue actions of sex steroids
rows: Fetal Wolffian ducts (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles); spermatogenesis via Sertoli cells; muscle mass; libido; laryngeal growth and voice deepening; erythropoiesis; LH feedback
Fetal external genitalia (penis, scrotum) and prostate; adult prostate growth; male-pattern scalp hair loss; beard and body hair; sebum production

Proliferative endometrium and induction of progesterone receptors; breast duct growth; thin, watery, stretchy cervical mucus; vaginal epithelial maturation; epiphyseal closure and bone preservation in both sexes; raised hepatic SHBG, thyroxine-binding globulin, angiotensinogen, and clotting factors; higher HDL and lower LDL

Secretory endometrium and decidualization; thick, scant cervical mucus; myometrial quiescence; breast lobuloalveolar development; slower GnRH pulses; raised ventilation; basal body temperature rise of about 0.3 to 0.5 °C (0.5 to 0.9 °F)
blocks.caption: DHT acts where 5-alpha-reductase is abundant; testosterone acts directly elsewhere; several bone and feedback effects in men require aromatization to estradiol.

blocks.text: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency shows the division clearly. A 46,XY infant has testes, normal anti-Mullerian hormone (so no uterus), and normal Wolffian derivatives because testosterone itself acts on the Wolffian ducts. The external genitalia, which need DHT, are undervirilized or appear female at birth, and the prostate is small. At puberty, the large rise in testosterone partly overcomes the defect and causes virilization of the genitalia and muscle, while scalp hair loss and acne are minimal. In complete androgen insensitivity, by contrast, the receptor itself fails, so neither testosterone nor DHT acts and Wolffian structures are absent.

Estrogen and progesterone act in sequence. Estrogen drives endometrial proliferation and induces progesterone receptors, so progesterone can act only on a primed endometrium; progesterone then converts it to a secretory lining suitable for implantation and opposes further proliferation. Unopposed estrogen, without cyclic progesterone, therefore causes endometrial hyperplasia. Progesterone raises the hypothalamic temperature set point, which is why the basal temperature rise confirms that ovulation has already occurred. Estrogen is also the main sex steroid that closes epiphyseal plates and restrains osteoclasts in both sexes, so men with aromatase or estrogen receptor deficiency remain tall with open epiphyses and low bone density despite normal testosterone.

sections.title: Puberty as reactivation of the GnRH pulse generator

blocks.text: The GnRH pulse generator is active in the fetus and again for several months after birth, a period called minipuberty, in which LH, FSH, and sex steroids rise briefly. Through childhood it is then held quiet by central inhibition, with gonadotropins low even though the pituitary and gonads can respond. Puberty begins when this restraint is lifted. Hypothalamic neurons that release kisspeptin and neurokinin B drive GnRH neurons through the KISS1R receptor, and loss of function mutations in kisspeptin signaling cause absent puberty. Adequate energy stores are permissive: leptin from adipose tissue signals that nutrition is sufficient, which is why severe undernutrition or very low body fat delays puberty.

The pulse generator wakes first during sleep. The earliest laboratory sign of puberty is the appearance of LH pulses in deep sleep, while daytime LH remains low; over the following years pulses spread across the whole day. Gonadal steroids then produce the physical changes. Adrenarche, the rise in adrenal androgens such as DHEA sulfate, is a separate process that is independent of GnRH and contributes to pubic and axillary hair.

blocks.title: Usual pubertal sequence
rows: Testicular enlargement to 4 mL or more, about age 9 to 14
Growth spurt (peak height velocity, early in puberty)
Growth spurt (later in puberty than in girls)
Menarche, about 2 to 3 years after thelarche
blocks.caption: Girls reach peak height velocity earlier in puberty than boys, which is one reason adult men are taller.

blocks.text: Each first sign has a mechanism. In girls, ovarian estradiol stimulates breast ducts before it has built enough endometrium to produce withdrawal bleeding, so breast budding precedes menarche, and early cycles are often anovulatory because the positive feedback mechanism matures last. In boys, FSH-driven growth of the seminiferous tubules, which make up most of testicular volume, enlarges the testes before testosterone produces visible virilization. Pubarche can occasionally come first in girls when adrenarche is early.

Measuring LH separates disorders of pubertal timing. Precocious puberty is usually defined as onset before about age 8 in girls and 9 in boys. In central (GnRH-dependent) precocious puberty, the pulse generator has started early, so LH is pubertal and rises after GnRH stimulation. In peripheral (GnRH-independent) precocious puberty, sex steroids come from the gonads, adrenals, or an outside source, so feedback suppresses LH and FSH.

Prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone whose dominant hypothalamic control is inhibitory. Tuberoinfundibular dopamine neurons release dopamine into the portal blood, and dopamine acts on D2 receptors on lactotrophs. D2 is coupled to Gi, so it lowers cAMP and opens K+ channels, which reduces prolactin synthesis, secretion, and lactotroph proliferation. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) and vasoactive intestinal peptide stimulate prolactin release, and estrogen increases lactotroph number and prolactin synthesis, which is why the pituitary enlarges in pregnancy. Prolactin regulates itself by short-loop feedback, raising hypothalamic dopamine release.

Because the normal signal is inhibitory, anything that blocks dopamine production, delivery, or action raises prolactin. The upper reference limit is about 20 to 25 ng/mL in women and somewhat lower in men, depending on the assay.

blocks.title: Mechanisms of hyperprolactinemia
rows: Autonomous secretion; level roughly tracks tumor size
Pituitary stalk compression by a nonsecreting mass
Dopamine cannot reach lactotrophs; usually a modest rise
blocks.caption: Pregnancy must be excluded first in any woman of reproductive age with a high prolactin.

blocks.text: High prolactin suppresses GnRH pulse release, largely by inhibiting kisspeptin neurons that drive GnRH neurons. LH and FSH therefore fall or remain inappropriately normal, and estradiol or testosterone falls. This is secondary (central) hypogonadism, and it has the same physiology as the normal lactational suppression of ovulation.

blocks.title: Prolactinoma to hypogonadism
steps: Lactotroph adenoma secretes excess prolactin
Prolactin inhibits kisspeptin neurons
GnRH pulse frequency and amplitude fall
LH and FSH low or inappropriately normal
Estradiol or testosterone falls
Amenorrhea, infertility, low libido, bone loss
blocks.caption: Hypogonadism in hyperprolactinemia is central: the gonads are normal but under-stimulated.

blocks.text: Women present with oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea, because prolactin acts on breast tissue already primed by estrogen. Men present with low libido, erectile dysfunction, and infertility; galactorrhea is uncommon and gynecomastia may occur. Women usually notice menstrual change early and so are found with small tumors, whereas men often are diagnosed later with macroadenomas that cause headache or bitemporal hemianopia by compressing the optic chiasm. Low estrogen in either sex reduces bone density.

blocks.predict: A woman with amenorrhea has a mildly raised prolactin, a high TSH, and a low free T4. What links the thyroid result to her prolactin?
blocks.explain: Low thyroid hormone removes feedback on the hypothalamus, so TRH rises. TRH stimulates lactotrophs as well as thyrotrophs, and the raised prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses, causing amenorrhea.
blocks.check: The table of hyperprolactinemia mechanisms and the paragraph on prolactin control.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology set the wiring. GnRH neurons originate in the olfactory placode, which is why failure of their migration links hypogonadism with anosmia in Kallmann syndrome, and the portal circulation explains why stalk compression raises prolactin while it can lower the other anterior pituitary hormones. In the gonads, the basement membrane that separates theca from granulosa cells and the blood-testis barrier formed by Sertoli cells explain why steroid synthesis is split between cell types and why spermatogenesis depends on locally concentrated testosterone. Biochemistry adds the enzymes, aromatase and 5-alpha-reductase, that decide which steroid acts in each tissue, and the hepatic synthesis of SHBG that ties reproductive hormones to insulin, thyroid hormone, and liver disease.

Pathology follows from feedback. A gonadal problem gives high gonadotropins with low steroids, a hypothalamic or pituitary problem gives low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins with low steroids, and exogenous steroid suppresses both LH and FSH. The limits are real: single hormone measurements miss pulsatility, total testosterone can mislead when SHBG changes, and reference ranges depend on age, sex, cycle phase, and assay, so values are read against the physiological state of the patient.

summary: Pulsatile GnRH stimulates LH and FSH through Gq signaling; continuous GnRH causes a brief flare, then receptor desensitization and low gonadotropins and sex steroids.
Fast GnRH pulses favor LH and slow pulses favor FSH.
LH drives Leydig cell testosterone; FSH drives Sertoli cell ABP, inhibin B, and aromatase; testosterone mainly suppresses LH and inhibin B selectively suppresses FSH.
Exogenous testosterone suppresses LH and FSH, lowers intratesticular testosterone, and causes testicular atrophy with poor spermatogenesis.
Theca cells (LH, CYP17) make androstenedione; granulosa cells (FSH, aromatase) convert it to estradiol.
Estradiol above about 200 pg/mL for about 2 days switches feedback to positive and triggers the LH surge; ovulation follows about 34 to 36 hours after surge onset.
Free plus albumin-bound testosterone is bioavailable; estrogen and thyroid hormone raise SHBG, while insulin, obesity, and androgens lower it and raise the free fraction.
DHT drives external genitalia, prostate, and male-pattern hair loss; testosterone drives Wolffian ducts, spermatogenesis, muscle, and libido; estrogen closes epiphyses in both sexes.
Puberty begins with sleep-associated LH pulses as kisspeptin reactivates GnRH; girls usually progress thelarche, pubarche, growth spurt, menarche.
Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin; hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH and causes amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and central hypogonadism.

verify: GnRH pulse intervals by cycle phase (about every 1 to 2 hours in the follicular phase, slower in the luteal phase) vary between sources; stated as approximate.
Testosterone binding fractions differ by source (free about 1 to 3%, albumin-bound about 30 to 55%, SHBG-bound the remainder in men); confirm the figures NABNE expects.
The intratesticular to serum testosterone ratio is quoted from about 25 to more than 100 fold; this chapter uses about 50 to 100 fold.

The estradiol threshold and duration for positive feedback (about 200 pg/mL for about 36 to 48 hours) and the surge to ovulation interval (about 34 to 36 hours) follow Guyton and Hall and common gynecologic references.

Ages for thelarche and testicular enlargement and the precocious puberty cutoffs (about 8 years in girls and 9 in boys) differ slightly by population and guideline; some sources use 7 years for some groups of girls.
Prolactin reference limits are assay dependent; confirm the cutoffs NABNE uses and whether it expects a stalk effect threshold (often quoted as below about 100 ng/mL).
Assignment of male-pattern hair loss mainly to the type 2 5-alpha-reductase isoenzyme follows common references; some texts emphasize contributions from type 1.

Requested new diagram name for a future revision: hpg-axis (hypothalamus, pituitary, testis and ovary with LH, FSH, steroid, and inhibin feedback arrows) and two-cell-follicle (theca and granulosa cells across the basement membrane).
